title: The great holocaust remembered
hookLine: Sikhs gather at Kup Rahira to remember 1762

cards: Flat fields, two villages, a road between them. On an ordinary day, the ground holds crops.
But on the day of remembrance, cars and buses pull in, and Sikhs walk out across the fields toward a memorial at Kup Rahira: grandparents, parents, small children on shoulders.
That's fitting, because what happened here happened to families. Sikhs call it the Vadda Ghallughara, the great holocaust. This path has told the day itself.

teach.h: A COLUMN CAUGHT IN THE OPEN.
teach.b: A slow column of Sikh families, the old and the young, was caught in the open by Ahmad Shah Abdali's army. The fighters with them formed a ring and kept the column moving, fighting on the outside.
The losses were terrible, and the old accounts don't agree on how many died. The remembrance doesn't turn on a figure. It turns on the people.
You might expect a war memory to put soldiers in the middle.

This one, in Sikh memory, puts the families there: the mothers, the children, the elders in the carts. The fighters are honored for one thing above all: they stayed between the danger and the ones who couldn't run.
A hymn draws the same shape.
On Ang 819, Guru Arjan sings, in paraphrase, that the hot wind does not touch the one under the Lord's shelter, and that all around is drawn the Lord's protecting circle, so pain cannot come near.
The hymn is about the shelter of the Name, not a battle. But a circle drawn around the vulnerable is the same picture the accounts of that day leave.

teach.h: A WEEK OF DAYS OF MEMORY.
teach.b: This week looked at chardi kala, sakhi, and your place in the story.
Then the calendar of memory began: reformers who did not strike back at Nankana, twenty-one names at Saragarhi, a garden at Vaisakhi, and now this field.
Each is kept with prayer and names, not with hatred for anyone living.

how: Sikhs remember the Vadda Ghallughara with Ardas and kirtan in gurdwaras, and some gather at Kup Rahira, where the families were caught, to remember those who died there.

games.q: it's the day of remembrance, and you've walked out to Kup Rahira with your family. who does the memory put at the center?
games.why: the families. the fighters are honored because they stayed between the danger and the ones who couldn't run.

practice: Bring to mind one family you know, your own, a neighbor's, a friend's, then let the circle widen to families anywhere who are on the move, in danger, or simply worn out, and keep them inside it for a while without trying to fix anything.
If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them, or hold the line from Ang 819 in your heart. If you don't, simply wish them shelter.
